performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
question: How does a first song set both a walking pace and a mood?
intro: The cycle opens with a departure at night: a steady march in the piano, a voice that arrives as a stranger and leaves as one, and a last verse that turns, briefly, to the major. Duhan’s 1928 recording fits it on one 78 rpm side by leaving out a verse.

sections.label: Verse 4 · the major, “Will dich im Traum nicht stören”

cues.title: A walking tempo
cues.text: The score is marked Mässig, in gehender Bewegung: moderate, in a walking motion. Six bars of repeated piano chords set the pace before the voice enters at about 0:14. Utz, summarising Youens, reads such repeated chords as a symbol of steps.
cues.evidence: The tempo marking, six bars of repeated quaver chords in the piano and the voice’s entry in bar 7 are in the OpenScore transcription (CC0). The report’s opening window is −21.4 dB with 1.8 attacks per second at 0:00. The entry is proportioned from the score’s 105 bars to the recording’s length, and a boundary falls at 0:16 (novelty 0.52). The step symbol is from Utz, ZGMTH 18 (2021), https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx, §2.

cues.title: A stranger arrives
cues.text: Müller’s first verse is a farewell. He came as a stranger and leaves as one. May was kind to him with many a bouquet; the girl spoke of love and her mother even of marriage. Now the world is dark and the road wrapped in snow.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 1, first stanza (1824 text on Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. The stanza is sung in bars 7–33 of the score (OpenScore), about 0:14–1:15 by proportion.

cues.title: Brighter for a moment
cues.text: Around 0:33 the music leaves the minor for the relative major, and the voice sings its phrase twice. The brightness lasts about twenty seconds. Then the minor closes in again.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:32 (novelty 0.69) and 0:46 (0.84); the local key estimate moves to a major reading at 0:40 (r 0.82), the relative major of the recording’s apparent minor key, after minor readings either side. The original D-minor score has the voice over F major and then B♭ major harmony in bars 15–23 and back in D minor from bar 25 (OpenScore). Times are proportioned, not aligned.

cues.title: The verse that is not sung
cues.text: In the second verse, which Duhan omits, the traveller says he cannot choose the time for his travels and must find his own way in the dark. A moon’s shadow goes with him as his companion, and on the white meadows he looks for the tracks of game.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 1, second stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. The printed score sets it by repeating bars 7–38; Utz’s footnote 25 records that Duhan and Foll omit this strophe (https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx).

cues.title: Straight to the third verse
cues.text: At about 1:26 the third verse begins: why linger until driven out? Let mad dogs howl before their master’s house; love loves to wander. The printed score repeats bars 7–38 first; Utz thinks the repeat was dropped for lack of room on one side.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:26 (novelty 1.00). Utz’s footnote 25 lists Duhan and Foll 1928 among five early recordings that omit the second strophe (bars 7–38, seconda volta), “probably” because the song would not fit on a side, and gives a measured length of 4:02 against a calculated 5:14 with the strophe (fn 83). In the score bar 39 sets “Was soll ich länger weilen” (OpenScore).

cues.title: A cycle of terrifying songs
cues.text: Schubert’s friend Joseph von Spaun recalled being told to come to Schober’s to hear “a cycle of terrifying songs”, which had affected Schubert more than any others. Schubert sang the whole of it. His friends were dumbfounded by its sombre mood.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Winterreise article, “Opinions of Schubert’s intentions”, quoting Spaun’s recollection (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterreise).

cues.title: The opening returns, then the major
cues.text: Before the last verse the piano plays the opening bars again, without the voice. Then, in the original D-minor score, the key signature changes to two sharps. Listen for the same steady chords now in the major.
cues.evidence: Quiet windows before the major are 2:30 (−23.0 dB, 0.2 attacks per second) and 2:35 (−25.4 dB); the key estimate reads minor to 2:30 and major from 2:40 (r 0.70–0.90), and the loudest window is 3:10 (−9.7 dB). The score has no voice in bars 66–70, which repeat bars 2–6, and a key signature of two sharps from bar 71 in the original D-minor score (OpenScore); the recording sounds lower. Times are proportioned.

cues.title: Good night on the gate
cues.text: In the last verse he will not disturb her dream or let her hear his step: softly, softly, close the door. As he passes he writes “good night” on her gate, so that she will see he thought of her.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Die Winterreise, no. 1, fourth stanza (Wikisource, https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Die_Winterreise_(Müller)), paraphrased. It is sung in bars 71–99 of the original score (OpenScore), about 2:40–3:46 by proportion.

cues.title: The first complete recording
cues.text: This is the earliest complete Winterreise on record, made in 1928, the centenary of Schubert’s death. Duhan recorded nineteen songs with the pianist Ferdinand Foll on 27 April, 2 and 4 May, and five more with Lene Orthmann in July. The cycle was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side.
cues.evidence: Utz, ZGMTH 18 (2021), §2 and its footnotes on the recording (https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx): the three dates with Foll, the five songs with Orthmann on 11 July, the set of twelve discs and one song per side.

cues.title: Back to the minor
cues.text: About 3:46 the minor returns for the last six bars, a postlude for the piano alone. The score slows slightly just before it. The chords go on walking and the song closes on a D minor chord in the score, with no word of arrival.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 3:46 (0.73), 3:50 (0.86) and 3:54 (0.94); the key estimate returns to minor at 3:50 and the level is −20.2 dB at 3:50. In the score the key signature of one flat returns at bar 99 after un poco ritard. at bar 98, and bars 100–105 are piano alone, ending on a D minor chord (OpenScore). The pitch of the transfer is not exact; no key is claimed for the recording.

transitions.title: The chords wait, then a voice
transitions.how: Six bars of repeated piano chords come first. The voice enters in bar 7 without any change of tempo or texture: its first phrase falls an octave over the same steady steps. Schubert does not set the voice against the piano. The walker’s pace belongs to the piano, and the singer takes it up.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 0:16 (novelty 0.52). The score has no voice in bars 1–6 and a voice entry in bar 7, F5 falling to F4 in the first phrase (OpenScore); the entry time is proportioned.

transitions.title: The second verse is not sung
transitions.how: The printed score repeats bars 7–38 for a second verse. In this recording the repeat is not taken, so the third verse follows the first at once, after a piano interlude of about five bars. The harmony is unchanged; the join is an elision of the repeat, and the third verse begins as the voice asks why it should linger.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:26 (1.00). Utz’s footnote 25 documents the omission of bars 7–38 by Duhan and Foll. The score has no voice in bars 34–38 and the third verse begins at bar 39 (OpenScore); the mapping is proportional.

transitions.title: Same steps, the major
transitions.how: After the third verse five bars of piano alone repeat the opening chords. At bar 71 the key signature changes to two sharps: the same walking chords, now in the major. The tempo and texture stay. The change is of colour only, and the last verse becomes a gentle goodnight at the beloved’s door, in place of the earlier bleakness.
transitions.evidence: Quiet windows are 2:30 (−23.0 dB, 0.2 attacks per second) and 2:35 (−25.4 dB); the key estimate reads minor to 2:30 and major from 2:40; a boundary falls at 2:38 (0.88). The score has no voice in bars 66–70 and two sharps from bar 71 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

transitions.title: Back to the minor, slowing
transitions.how: After a held last line the score slows slightly, and at bar 99 the key signature of one flat returns with a tempo. The major of the last verse has been a dream within the song. The six bars of postlude let the chords walk on and settle on a minor chord without a gesture of farewell.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 3:46 (0.73), 3:50 (0.86) and 3:54 (0.94); the key estimate returns to minor at 3:50. The score marks un poco ritard. at bar 98 and a tempo with one flat from bar 99 (OpenScore); times are proportioned.

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 1, Gute Nacht, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: bars 1–105; the voice is silent in bars 1–6, 34–38, 66–70 and 100–105 (the seconda volta, bars 7–38, is not sung in this recording); times proportioned to the boundaries at 0:16, 1:26, 2:38 and 3:46.

timeline.note: The piano alone sets the walking pace.
The voice enters over the steady chords.
A short piano interlude, then the third verse.
The piano repeats the opening bars alone.
The last verse, in the major.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Abridged: the second strophe, bars 7–38 (the seconda volta), is not sung; the song runs about 4:02
fields.note: Utz lists Duhan and Foll 1928 among five early recordings that omit the second strophe, probably because the song would not otherwise fit on one side, and gives a measured length of 4:02 against a calculated 5:14 with the strophe. The key, any transposition and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: His Master’s Voice, as printed on the scanned copy (manufactured by The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited, Ústí nad Labem)
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of the later discs (3, 6, 12) carry Gramola Record labels, so the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 383, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CK 2946, take 2 (run-out “Ck 2946” with II); side No. 1 (label number 0942026); reverse side: Die Wetterfahne (matrix CK 2947-2). Disc 1 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (249.00 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (248.85 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
